title: The Deep
subtitle: Pressure, tides, reefs and the creatures of the dark
subject: Oceans

pages.h: A planet with the wrong name
p: We call it Earth, but from space it is mostly blue. Water covers 71 percent of the surface. Almost all of it, 97 percent, is ocean: about 1.3 billion cubic kilometres of salt water. If you could flatten every mountain and fill every valley, the sea would cover the whole planet 2.7 kilometres deep.

The ocean is also deep in a way land is not high. Its average depth is about 3,700 metres. Mount Everest reaches 8,849 metres above sea level, but the deepest point in the sea is 10,935 metres down. Drop Everest into it and the summit would still be 2 kilometres underwater.

Because it is so deep, the ocean holds more than 99 percent of the space on Earth where life can live. Land animals, including you, live on a thin skin. Most of the living room on this planet is cold, dark and wet, and we have barely started to look at it. This book goes down.
pages.cap: From orbit, the name is obvious: it should have been called Ocean.
pages.fact: Did you know? There is more gold dissolved in sea water than has ever been mined, but it is so spread out that nobody can collect it.

pages.h: Why the sea is salty and blue
p: Scoop up a kilogram of sea water and boil it away. You are left with about 35 grams of salt, mostly the same sodium chloride you put on chips. Where did it come from? Rain is slightly acidic, and for billions of years it has been dissolving tiny amounts of rock and carrying them down rivers. Rivers taste fresh because the salt is so dilute, but the sea has no outlet. Water evaporates and leaves; salt stays. Spread all the ocean's salt over the land, and it would make a layer 150 metres thick.

The blue is not a reflection of the sky. Water itself is faintly blue. It absorbs red light much more than blue, so sunlight going down loses its red within about 10 metres, then orange, then yellow. A cut at 20 metres bleeds green-black blood. By 200 metres, only a dim blue remains. Below that, nothing. The sea is blue because it eats every other colour.
pages.cap: Salt dissolved from rocks over billions of years, carried by rivers, left behind by evaporation.

pages.h: We have better maps of the surface of Mars than of our own sea floor.
p: By 2025, only about a quarter of the ocean bottom had been measured in detail. The rest is a blurry guess from satellites.

pages.h: Going down: the five zones
p: Dive from the surface and the ocean changes in layers. The top 200 metres is the sunlight zone. Light reaches here, plants and plankton can grow, and this is where nearly all the fish you have eaten lived. It is a thin lid: only about 5 percent of the ocean's volume.

From 200 to 1,000 metres is the twilight zone. There is a faint blue glow from above but not enough for plants. From 1,000 to 4,000 metres is the midnight zone: total darkness, water near 4 degrees Celsius, and the only light is made by animals. From 4,000 to 6,000 metres is the abyss, the flat muddy plains that cover more than half the planet.

Below 6,000 metres are the trenches, the hadal zone, named after Hades, the Greek underworld. They are narrow cracks where one piece of Earth's crust slides under another. Together they are only about 1 percent of the sea floor, but they hold the deepest 45 percent of the ocean's depth range.
pages.cap: Like the planet itself, the ocean comes in layers: sunlight, twilight, midnight, abyss, and the trenches below.

pages.h: The weight of water
p: Every 10 metres you go down, the water above you adds another full atmosphere of pressure, as much as all the air above your head at the surface. At 10 metres the pressure is doubled. At 100 metres it is 11 times normal. At 1,000 metres, where sperm whales hunt, it is 100 times normal. At the bottom of the deepest trench, the pressure is about 1,100 atmospheres: 1,100 kilograms pressing on every square centimetre, like an elephant standing on a postage stamp.

Lower a foam coffee cup to 3,000 metres and bring it back, and it comes up the size of a thimble, perfectly shaped, because the air bubbles in the foam were crushed. Deep-sea animals avoid this by having no air inside. Their bodies are mostly water, which barely squeezes, so the pressure pushes equally from all sides and they feel nothing. Bring them up too fast, though, and some fall apart, because their proteins were built for a world where they are always being squeezed.
pages.cap: A boat sits on the surface, but the water pressing on a sinking stone grows by one atmosphere every 10 metres.

pages.q: A diver goes down to 30 metres. How much pressure is on her compared with the surface?
pages.why: Each 10 metres adds one atmosphere; 30 metres adds three, plus the one from the air above, so four altogether.

pages.h: The deepest place on Earth
p: In the western Pacific, near the island of Guam, the sea floor drops into the Mariana Trench. Its lowest point, Challenger Deep, is about 10,935 metres down. A steel ball dropped from the surface would take over an hour to reach the bottom. Sunlight gives up after 1 percent of the way. The water is near 2 degrees Celsius, and the pressure is 1,100 times what you feel now.

Only three people visited before 2019: two in the bathyscaphe Trieste in 1960, and film director James Cameron alone in 2012. Then a submarine built to go there again and again, Limiting Factor, began making dives, and dozens of people have now been. They found a pale, flat floor of mud, strange sea cucumbers, shrimp-like amphipods the size of a hand, and a plastic bag.
The trench exists because the Pacific plate is sliding under the Philippine plate here, dragging the sea floor down with it. It is a crack in the planet's skin, 2,550 kilometres long.
pages.cap: Where one plate dives under another, the sea floor is dragged down into a trench.

pages.h: Tides: the Moon pulling the sea
p: Twice a day, on most coasts, the sea rises and then slides back. The puller is the Moon. Its gravity tugs on Earth, and the ocean on the side facing the Moon is pulled a little more than the planet's centre, so it bulges toward the Moon. On the far side, the water is pulled a little less than the centre, so it is left behind in a second bulge. Earth spins under both bulges once a day: two high tides, two low tides.
The Moon moves a bit each day, so the tides come about 50 minutes later every day. When the Sun and Moon line up, at full and new moon, their pulls add together and tides are extra big: spring tides.

The size depends on the shape of the coast. In the open ocean the tide is less than a metre. In the Bay of Fundy, between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, the bay's shape makes the water slosh, and the difference between high and low tide reaches 16 metres, the height of a five-storey building.
pages.cap: Full and new moon: the Sun and Moon pull together, and the tides reach their highest and lowest.

pages.h: Try it: make a river float on the sea
p: Salt water and fresh water do not mix easily. See the layer.
steps: Fill a clear glass halfway with warm tap water. Stir in three heaped spoons of salt until it dissolves. Add a few drops of blue food colouring.
Fill a second glass with cold fresh water and add a drop of red colouring.
Very slowly pour the red water onto the blue, over the back of a spoon held just above the surface, so it trickles in gently.

Watch: the red fresh water floats on the blue salty water in a layer. Salty water is denser and sinks, which is exactly what happens where rivers meet the sea, and what drives the deep ocean currents.
Now stir hard. The layers mix. Leave it for an hour: do they separate again?
pages.cap: Dense salt water sinks beneath lighter fresh water. Oceans are stacked like this too.
pages.safe: Food colouring stains; wear old clothes and work on a tray.

pages.h: Rivers inside the sea
p: The ocean is not still water. It is crossed by currents, rivers of sea flowing through the sea. The biggest near Canada is the Gulf Stream, which pours out of the Gulf of Mexico, past Florida, and across the Atlantic. At its widest it carries about 150 million cubic metres of water every second, more than a hundred times the flow of all the rivers on Earth put together, at a speed of up to 9 kilometres per hour. Its warm water is part of why Britain, farther north than most Canadians live, has mild winters.

Surface currents are mostly pushed by wind. Because Earth spins, moving water curves: to the right in the northern hemisphere, to the left in the southern. The result is giant circles called gyres, one in each ocean basin. The North Pacific gyre is where floating plastic collects into the 'garbage patch', a region larger than Ontario where tiny plastic bits are scattered through the water like confetti.
pages.cap: Sailing ships crossing the Atlantic rode the Gulf Stream east and the trade winds west.

pages.h: The great conveyor belt
p: Underneath the wind-driven currents is a slower, deeper flow. Near Greenland and in the seas around Antarctica, surface water gets very cold and very salty, because sea ice forming there leaves salt behind. Cold salty water is heavy. It sinks, kilometres down, and creeps along the sea floor toward the equator and beyond. Somewhere far away, perhaps in the Indian or Pacific Ocean, it slowly rises again and begins the long return at the surface.

One drop of water takes about 1,000 years to make the full loop. This conveyor belt moves heat from the tropics toward the poles and carries oxygen down to the deep sea. Without it, the deep ocean would suffocate.

Scientists are watching the Atlantic part of the belt closely. Some measurements suggest it has weakened by about 15 percent since the 1950s, as melting ice adds fresh water that is too light to sink. Whether it could slow dramatically this century is one of the most argued questions in ocean science.
pages.cap: Heat goes up, cold salty water goes down: the ocean has a slow circulation of its own.

pages.h: Waves: energy that passes through
p: A wave is not water travelling. It is energy travelling through water. Watch a gull floating on a swell: it bobs up and down and ends up where it started. The wind piles up the surface, and the bump passes along, water circling in place as it goes.

Most waves are made by wind. The longer and harder it blows across open sea, the bigger they grow. In the Southern Ocean, where wind circles the globe with no land in the way, waves of 10 metres are normal, and a buoy near New Zealand recorded one of 23.8 metres in 2018.

Rogue waves were thought to be sailors' tales until 1995, when a platform in the North Sea measured a wall of water 25.6 metres high, twice the waves around it. Tsunamis are different again: made by earthquakes, they are only a metre high at sea but race at 800 kilometres per hour, as fast as a jet, and when they reach shallow coasts they slow down, bunch up, and rise into a wall.
pages.cap: Storm winds pile up the sea; the energy races on while the water stays behind.

pages.q: What makes the deep ocean conveyor belt sink near Greenland?
pages.why: Cold water is denser, and freezing sea ice leaves extra salt behind, so the water becomes heavy enough to sink kilometres.

pages.h: The invisible forest
p: There is a forest in the ocean, and you cannot see a single tree. It is made of phytoplankton: drifting cells, most of them smaller than the width of a hair, that do what leaves do. They take sunlight, water and dissolved carbon dioxide and make sugar, releasing oxygen. There are so many of them that they produce about half of all the oxygen on Earth. Every second breath you take came from the sea.

Some are glass. Diatoms build shells of silica in patterns like snowflakes and lace. Some are chalk. When they die, their shells rain to the bottom, and over millions of years they become rock; the white cliffs of England are mostly plankton.

They are also the bottom of nearly every ocean food chain. Tiny animals called zooplankton eat them, small fish eat those, and so on up to tuna and whales. Antarctic krill, finger-length shrimp that eat plankton, add up to about 400 million tonnes, roughly the mass of all the humans on Earth.
pages.cap: Drifting single cells, each a tiny solar panel, make half the planet's oxygen.

pages.h: Coral: an animal that builds cities
p: A coral reef looks like rock covered in colourful plants. It is neither. Coral is an animal, a tiny soft polyp like a miniature sea anemone, and a reef is millions of them, each sitting in a cup of limestone it built itself. Inside each polyp live even tinier algae. The algae use sunlight to make sugar and give most of it to the coral; the coral gives the algae a safe home and its waste as fertilizer. The colour you see is the algae.

Reefs grow slowly, about 1 centimetre a year, and only in warm, clear, shallow water. The Great Barrier Reef, off Australia, is 2,300 kilometres long and the largest structure built by living things, visible from orbit.

Reefs cover less than 0.1 percent of the sea floor, yet about a quarter of all ocean species live on them. They are the cities of the sea: crowded, noisy with snapping shrimp, and built from the bones of their own ancestors.
pages.cap: Each coral head is a colony of thousands of tiny animals, built on the skeletons of the ones before.

pages.h: Bleaching: when the city empties
p: Corals live close to the edge. If the water stays about 1 degree Celsius warmer than their summer normal for several weeks, the partnership breaks down. The algae start making poisons, and the coral throws them out. Without the algae the coral is transparent, so you see its white limestone skeleton through it: bleaching. The coral is not dead yet, but it is starving.
If the water cools within a few weeks, algae move back in and the coral recovers. If the heat lasts, it dies, and in a year the skeleton is fuzzy with seaweed.

The ocean has absorbed most of the planet's extra heat, and reefs are feeling it first. A global bleaching event that began in 2023 hit about 84 percent of the world's reefs by 2025, the worst on record. Some corals, in the Red Sea and parts of the Pacific, are proving tougher than others, and scientists are trying to understand why, and whether that toughness can be bred or spread.
pages.cap: A bleached reef: still alive, but starving, until the water cools or it does not.

pages.h: Half of the oxygen you breathe was made by plankton too small to see.
p: Thank a diatom. Then thank the ocean that is holding most of the planet's extra heat so that the air does not have to.

pages.h: The largest migration on Earth, every night
p: Every evening, as the sun sets, something enormous happens in the twilight zone. Billions of tonnes of small animals, lanternfish, shrimp, squid and jelly, rise from 500 metres or deeper toward the surface to feed in the dark, then sink back before dawn to hide from daytime hunters. It is the biggest movement of animals on the planet, and it happens every single day. Sonar operators in the Second World War saw the 'sea floor' rising at dusk and could not understand it.

Lanternfish, finger-length fish with rows of lights along their bellies, are probably the most numerous vertebrates on Earth; their total mass may be several billion tonnes, far more than all the fish people catch.

This daily elevator does a job for the planet. The animals eat near the surface, then carry carbon down in their bodies and their droppings, sinking it into the deep for centuries. Nobody knows exactly how much, which is why ships now circle the oceans with nets and sonar trying to count.
pages.cap: Plankton feeds lanternfish, lanternfish feed everything else, and the whole crowd rides up and down each night.

pages.h: Making your own light
p: Below 1,000 metres the sun is gone, but the sea is full of sparks. About three-quarters of deep-sea animals can make their own light: bioluminescence. They do it with a chemical reaction, a molecule called luciferin and an enzyme, that gives off light without heat. Most of the glow is blue, because blue travels farthest through water.

The uses are clever. The anglerfish dangles a glowing lure in front of its mouth, lit by bacteria living inside it, and waits for a curious fish. Hatchetfish have lights on their bellies tuned to match the faint glow from above, so a hunter below sees no silhouette. Some shrimp spit a cloud of glowing goo at attackers and escape behind it. Flashlight fish blink to talk to each other.

At the surface, tiny plankton flash when disturbed, so a swimmer at night can trail sparks. Why some deep animals glow is still unknown. For many species, scientists have seen the light but have no idea what it is for.
pages.cap: An anglerfish's lure: a bulb of glowing bacteria on a fishing rod made of bone.

pages.h: Giants in the dark
p: The giant squid was a sea-monster story for centuries. Dead ones washed ashore, up to 13 metres long with eyes the size of dinner plates, the largest eyes of any animal. But no one saw one alive in its home until 2012, when a camera 630 metres down off Japan filmed one hunting. Its heavier cousin, the colossal squid of the Antarctic, weighs up to 500 kilograms and has rotating hooks on its arms. A live one was filmed for the first time only in March 2025: a baby 30 centimetres long.

Their main enemy is the sperm whale, which dives to 2,000 metres and holds its breath for up to 90 minutes to hunt them, finding them in the blackness with clicks of sound. Whale skins are often scarred with sucker rings.

Other giants are gentler. The Greenland shark grows a centimetre a year and can live 400 years; one swimming today may have been born before Canada existed. The Japanese spider crab spans 3.7 metres, claw to claw.
pages.cap: Somewhere in the dark below, a 13-metre squid with dinner-plate eyes is watching for a whale.

pages.q: Why is most deep-sea bioluminescence blue?
opts: Blue is the easiest colour for chemicals to make
Blue light travels farthest through water, so it can be seen from farther away
Deep-sea animals cannot see other colours
pages.why: Water absorbs red and yellow quickly; blue goes farthest, so blue signals and lures work best in the deep.

pages.h: Hot springs on the sea floor
p: In 1977, scientists in a tiny submarine near the Galapagos Islands, 2,500 metres down, found something that should not have existed. Water hot enough to melt lead was gushing from chimneys of black rock, and around them, in total darkness, crowded a city of animals: 2-metre red tube worms, white crabs, clams the size of dinner plates. No sunlight had ever reached this place. What were they eating?

The answer rewrote biology. Sea water seeps into cracks in the crust, is heated by magma to 400 degrees Celsius, and shoots back out loaded with dissolved minerals and a gas called hydrogen sulphide. Bacteria eat that gas, making sugar from chemicals instead of light. Chemosynthesis. The tube worms have no mouths; they are stuffed with the bacteria and live off them.

Vents have been found in every ocean since, some 5,000 metres down. Many scientists think life itself may have started at a vent four billion years ago, and that similar vents on the icy moons of Jupiter and Saturn might be the best places to look for life beyond Earth.
pages.cap: Sea water meets magma and blasts back out at 400 degrees, feeding animals that never see the Sun.

pages.h: Life at the very bottom
p: How deep can a fish live? In 2023, a camera on a lander near Japan filmed a snailfish swimming at 8,336 metres, the deepest fish ever seen. It was pale, soft, almost jelly, with a body built so that the crushing pressure pushes in equally from every side. Scientists think fish cannot live much below about 8,400 metres, because the chemical they use to keep their proteins from being crushed cannot be packed any tighter.

Below that, other animals take over. Amphipods, shrimp-like scavengers, swarm over any food that falls, some grown to 30 centimetres in the deepest trenches. Sea cucumbers plod across the mud eating it. Single-celled creatures called xenophyophores grow as large as a fist, the biggest single cells on Earth.
Food down there is whatever sinks: a dead whale can feed a patch of sea floor for 50 years. Most of the time, the deep is a slow place. A trench amphipod may wait months between meals.
pages.cap: A xenophyophore is a single cell, like this one, but as big as your fist.

pages.h: The ocean's quiet job
p: The ocean is doing the planet a favour you never see. Since the 1800s, people have been burning coal, oil and gas, and about a quarter of the carbon dioxide released has dissolved into sea water. Even more important, more than 90 percent of the extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases has gone into the ocean. If it had gone into the air instead, the surface of Earth would be tens of degrees hotter. The ocean has been absorbing the shock.

There is a cost. Carbon dioxide in water makes a weak acid. The ocean's pH has dropped from about 8.2 to 8.1 since the 1800s, which sounds tiny but means 30 percent more acid. Shelled animals, from corals to the tiny sea butterflies that salmon eat, have to work harder to build their shells, and some are thinning.
Warmer water also holds less oxygen and expands, which, together with melting ice, is why sea level has risen about 25 centimetres since 1900, and is now rising about 4 millimetres a year.
pages.cap: Heat flows from the air into the sea, and the sea has taken nine-tenths of the extra.

pages.h: Try it: a cold current in a glass
p: Make a miniature deep-ocean current with ice.
steps: The day before, freeze an ice cube with a few drops of blue food colouring mixed into the water.
Fill a clear bowl or large glass with warm tap water and let it settle for a minute.
Float the blue ice cube at one edge of the bowl. Do not stir.
Watch the blue meltwater: it is cold and dense, so it sinks to the bottom and creeps across the floor of the bowl, just as water chilled near Greenland sinks and slides toward the equator.
Try it again with a spoon of salt dissolved in the warm water first. Does the blue sink faster or slower? Why?
pages.cap: Melting ice makes cold water that sinks; the same thing drives currents around the world.
pages.safe: Use warm, not hot, water: nothing that could scald.

pages.h: Ice at the ends of the Earth
p: At both poles, the sea freezes. Arctic sea ice is a floating lid 1 to 4 metres thick that grows every winter and shrinks every summer. Since satellites started watching in 1979, the summer ice has shrunk by about 40 percent, an area larger than Quebec, and the ice that remains is younger and thinner. Polar bears hunt from it; without it, they starve. Bright ice also reflects sunlight back to space; dark open water absorbs it, so losing ice makes the Arctic warm faster, a loop that feeds itself.

Antarctica is the opposite: ice on land, with floating shelves at its edges. The ice there is 2 kilometres thick on average and holds enough water to raise the sea by about 58 metres if it all melted. It will not, not for thousands of years, but its edges are crumbling faster than expected.

Icebergs are broken-off pieces. Only about one-tenth shows above water. The largest in recent years, A23a, was about 3,900 square kilometres when it broke free: six times the area of the city of Toronto.
pages.cap: Nine-tenths of an iceberg hides below the surface, which is what sank the Titanic.

pages.h: The loudest quiet place
p: The deep ocean is dark, but it is not silent. Sound travels through water at about 1,500 metres per second, four times faster than through air, and it carries much farther. About 1,000 metres down there is a layer, the deep sound channel, where sound waves get trapped and bend back toward the middle, so a noise there can travel thousands of kilometres. A blue whale's call, at 188 decibels, louder than a jet engine, can in theory be heard by another whale across an entire ocean.

Whales live by sound. Sperm whales find squid with clicks. Humpbacks sing songs that last 20 minutes and change from year to year, like fashions, and nobody knows what they mean. Even coral reefs have a sound, a crackle of shrimp claws and fish grunts that baby fish drifting at sea use to find their way home.
Ships, drilling and sonar have made the oceans much noisier in the last century. For an animal that sees with its ears, that is like living in fog.
pages.cap: Underwater, sound travels four times faster and far farther than in air.

pages.q: What has absorbed most of the extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases?
pages.why: More than 90 percent of the extra heat has gone into sea water, which is why the ocean is warming and expanding.

pages.h: What the ocean does for you
p: Even if you live far from any coast, you depend on the sea every day. The ocean stores heat in summer and releases it in winter, and it feeds every cloud, so it shapes the weather over Winnipeg as surely as over Halifax. About 3 billion people get a large part of their protein from seafood, and fishing boats haul in roughly 90 million tonnes a year, so much that about a third of fish stocks are now being caught faster than they can breed.

Ships carry about 80 percent of everything the world trades: the phone, the shoes, the bananas. More than 95 percent of international internet traffic runs not through satellites but through about 1.4 million kilometres of fibre-optic cable lying on the sea floor.

And the ocean is a medicine cabinet. A chemical from a Caribbean sponge became a drug for leukemia; cone snail venom became a painkiller. Thousands of sea creatures have never been tested. Some have never even been named.
pages.cap: A city far from the coast still runs on ocean weather, ocean cargo and ocean cables.

pages.h: Mapping the blind spot
p: Here is a strange fact: we know the shape of the Moon's far side better than the shape of the ocean floor. Satellites can measure the sea surface and guess at the mountains beneath from tiny bulges in the water, but that guess is blurry, missing anything smaller than a few kilometres. Measuring properly means a ship or robot pinging the bottom with sound, strip by strip. By 2025, about 27 percent of the sea floor had been mapped this way. A project called Seabed 2030 is trying to finish the job, and will probably not make it on time.

The tools are changing. Robot submarines now cruise for months on their own, mapping and sniffing for vents. Floats called Argo, about 4,000 of them, drift through the oceans measuring temperature and salt and surfacing to report by satellite. Cameras on landers sit on trench floors waiting for whatever comes.
Each year brings a few thousand new species. Scientists guess that most ocean species, maybe 90 percent, have still never been seen.
pages.cap: We mapped the Moon through telescopes centuries ago; the sea floor, hidden under kilometres of water, is harder.

pages.h: What we still do not know
p: The deep ocean is the biggest unknown on the planet, and honest scientists say so. Nobody knows how many species live there; guesses run from several hundred thousand to over a million. Nobody knows exactly how much carbon the nightly migration of animals carries down, which matters for predicting climate. Nobody knows whether the Atlantic conveyor belt will slow a little or a lot this century.
Nobody knows what humpback whales are singing about, or why the songs change. Nobody knows how some corals survive heat that kills their neighbours.

And there are new questions. Countries are deciding whether to mine the abyssal plains for metal lumps that take millions of years to grow and are home to animals found nowhere else; the first commercial permits were being argued over in 2025. Whether the deep can recover from that, no one can say, because no one has watched it try. The ocean has kept most of its secrets. The next few decades will decide which ones we learn, and which we lose.
pages.cap: Abyssal mud piles up about a centimetre every thousand years, recording what fell from above.

pages.h: The deep sea is the largest living space on Earth, and we have looked at less than 1 percent of it.
p: Every dive finds something new. Most of the planet is still waiting to be met.

qs: If most of the ocean's species have never been seen, how should we decide whether to mine the deep sea floor?
Humans have been to the deepest point in the ocean, but far fewer times than to the top of Everest. Why do you think the deep gets less attention?
The ocean has been soaking up our extra heat and carbon dioxide. Do we owe it something in return? What?
